content: Measurement bias may be present in the other studies. In the study by Jackson (2004), infants who were randomly assigned to receive phenobarbitone were more likely to have been exposed to benzodiazepines and other classes of drugs compared to those randomized to receive morphine. Statistical heterogeneity was not observed in this analysis (I² = 0%). The combined sample size across the studies is 302 participants. However, the event rate is very low. Although the confidence interval is narrow, according to GRADE criteria for dichotomous data, event rates below 300 are downgraded for imprecision. The randomized controlled trial (RCT) by Kandall (1983) was assessed to have an unclear risk of selection bias because no method of random sequence generation was reported. The randomized groups were highly imbalanced (49 participants in one group versus 62 in the other), which increases the likelihood of selection bias. Detection and performance bias may also be present, as no blinding was reported. Attrition was not reported, and the risk of selective reporting was unclear. The sample size in some studies is small, and the event rate is very low (e.g., zero events in the opioid group), with wide confidence intervals. Two studies included in this meta-analysis (Khoo 1995 and Madden 1977) were quasi-randomized trials. These studies carry a high risk of selection bias due to inadequate random sequence generation and allocation concealment. Blinding was not reported, leading to an unclear risk of detection and performance bias. Both studies accounted for incomplete outcome data, so attrition bias was judged to be low. However, selective reporting bias remained unclear. The quasi-RCT by Khoo (1995) was judged to have a high risk of selection bias because randomization was based on the last digit of the participant's hospital number, and allocation concealment was inadequate. Blinding was not reported, and performance and detection bias may be present. The sample size was small, and the confidence interval was wide. The guidelines for the identification and management of substance use and substance use disorders in pregnancy highlight that the meta-analysis included one quasi-trial (Finnegan 1984) and one RCT (Madden 1977). GRADE assessment was conducted within the RCT study design category. Madden (1977) was judged to have an unclear risk of selection bias due to the lack of reported random sequence generation or allocation concealment. Blinding was not reported, so performance and detection bias may be present. Incomplete outcome data were addressed, so attrition bias was minimal. The meta-analysis combined two quasi-trials (Finnegan 1984 and Kaltenbach 1986). It was unclear whether some infants reported in the study were also included in Finnegan (1984), raising the risk of double-counting participants. Allocation concealment was judged to be inadequate, and there is a high risk of selection bias. Blinding was not clearly reported for short-term outcomes, and the treatment regimens were different, leading to a high risk of performance and detection bias. Selective reporting of outcomes was unclear and could not be judged. Statistical heterogeneity was present in some analyses (e.g., I² = 85%), and the heterogeneity was unexplained. This was downgraded for unexplained inconsistency. The sample size in many studies was small, with low event rates and wide confidence intervals. In some cases, no method of random sequence generation was reported, and allocation concealment was unlikely, leading to a high risk of selection bias. Blinding was not reported, and performance and detection bias may be present. However, incomplete outcome data were accounted for, so attrition bias was low. The meta-analysis also included a quasi-RCT (Khoo 1995) and an RCT (Jackson 2004). In Khoo (1995), there was a high risk of selection bias due to inadequate random sequence generation and allocation concealment. Blinding was not performed for treatment and not reported for assessment, so performance and detection bias may be present. Jackson (2004) was well-conducted and at low risk of selection, performance, and detection bias. However, the GRADE assessment was conducted according to the lower quality of evidence, so the analysis was downgraded for bias. Statistical heterogeneity was not present in some analyses, and there did not appear to be unexplained clinical heterogeneity. However, in other cases, statistical heterogeneity was observed (e.g., I² = 67%), and the heterogeneity was unexplained. This was downgraded for unexplained inconsistency. Although the confidence interval was narrow in some cases, the analysis was downgraded for imprecision due to the small sample size and low event rate. The guidelines for the identification and management of substance use and substance use disorders in pregnancy emphasize that treatment failure was defined as the failure to reduce a standardized score of neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) from a clinically significant level to a clinically safe level, as defined by the trial author, or the use of additional pharmacological treatments for NAS control. The meta-analysis combined results from two RCTs (Jackson 2004 and Madden 1977) and two quasi-randomized trials (Finnegan 1984 and Khoo 1995). Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were lacking in three of the four studies, leading to a risk of selection bias. Blinding of participants and providers was only performed in one study, so performance and measurement bias may be present in the other studies.
